common_name: Arctic Gold Daffodil (Golden Yellow Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Arctic Gold is a sturdy, all-gold trumpet daffodil bred in the Netherlands and prized for its dependable, uniform mid-season display.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Arctic Gold is a Division 1 trumpet daffodil bearing a rich, uniform golden-yellow perianth and trumpet with a smooth, slightly flanged rim, opening on strong, weather-resistant stems in mid-season. Bred in the Netherlands, it was selected for exceptional garden vigor and consistency of form, making it a workhorse variety for mass plantings, borders, and naturalizing in turf. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, since it recharges the bulb for next year's flowers, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply into dense drifts.

common_name: Unsurpassable Daffodil (Giant Golden Yellow Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Unsurpassable is an old Dutch trumpet daffodil noted for its unusually large, heavy golden blooms on tall stems.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Unsurpassable is a Division 1 trumpet daffodil bred in the Netherlands, producing some of the largest flowers of any trumpet cultivar, with a deep golden-yellow perianth and a broad, gently flared trumpet of matching color. Its exceptional size and heavy substance made it a standard exhibition and cut-flower variety through much of the twentieth century, and it remains a reliable garden bulb where its tall stems can be given some shelter from strong wind. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply and naturalize over time.

common_name: Mrs. R.O. Backhouse Daffodil (Historic Pink-Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Mrs. R.O. Backhouse, registered in 1921, was the first daffodil ever offered commercially with pink coloring in the trumpet.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Mrs. R.O. Backhouse is a Division 1 trumpet daffodil bred by English horticulturist Sarah Backhouse and introduced in 1921 as the first pink-toned daffodil ever put into commerce, bearing a creamy white perianth around a long trumpet that opens pale yellow and matures to a soft apricot-pink, especially in cool weather. Though pale by the standard of modern pink cultivars it developed from, it remains historically significant as the parent of virtually all later pink-cupped daffodils and is still grown by collectors of heirloom bulbs. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply.

common_name: Empress of Ireland Daffodil (Giant Pure White Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Empress of Ireland is a Guy Wilson-bred giant white trumpet daffodil considered one of the finest all-white trumpets ever raised.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Empress of Ireland is a Division 1 trumpet daffodil bred by renowned Northern Irish hybridizer Guy L. Wilson, bearing enormous, substantial flowers of pure glistening white from broad overlapping perianth segments to a wide, smooth-rimmed trumpet, with none of the creamy or greenish cast common in earlier white trumpets. It flowers in mid-season on tall, sturdy stems and has long been ranked among the finest exhibition white trumpets raised in the twentieth century. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over the years.

common_name: Fortissimo Daffodil (Yellow Large-Cupped Daffodil with Orange-Red Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Fortissimo is a vigorous Dutch large-cupped daffodil with a bold contrast of golden-yellow petals and a flat, fiery orange-red cup.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall. Fortissimo is a Division 2 large-cupped daffodil bred in the Netherlands, bearing broad golden-yellow perianth segments surrounding a flat, frilled cup of intense orange-red that holds its color well as the bloom ages. It is an unusually vigorous and floriferous cultivar with tall, strong stems, making it a favorite for cutting as well as mass garden display. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, since it recharges the bulb for next year's flowers, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply.

common_name: Passionale Daffodil (White Large-Cupped Daffodil with Pink Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Passionale is a popular Dutch large-cupped daffodil with a clean white perianth and a rose-pink cup that deepens as it ages.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall. Passionale is a Division 2 large-cupped daffodil bred in the Netherlands, with broad, rounded white perianth segments surrounding a cup that opens pale apricot-pink and deepens to a warmer rose-pink as the flower matures and is exposed to sun. It is one of the more reliable and widely grown pink-cupped daffodils, valued for its clean color, sturdy stems, and good naturalizing habit in cooler climates. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over time.

common_name: Ceylon Daffodil (Golden Yellow Large-Cupped Daffodil with Red-Orange Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Ceylon is a De Graaff-bred large-cupped daffodil with rich golden petals and a flat red-orange cup, a long-time exhibition favorite.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall. Ceylon is a Division 2 large-cupped daffodil bred by the Dutch firm of de Graaff, bearing rounded, deep golden-yellow perianth segments around a flat, frilled cup of bright red-orange that contrasts sharply with the petals. Its bold color combination, smooth flower form, and strong stems made it a long-running favorite on the show bench as well as in garden borders. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply.

common_name: Liberty Bells Daffodil (Pale Yellow Nodding Triandrus Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Liberty Bells is a Grant Mitsch-bred Triandrus daffodil bearing two to three nodding, pale lemon-yellow flowers per stem.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Liberty Bells is a Triandrus-type (Division 5) daffodil bred by Oregon hybridizer Grant Mitsch, bearing clusters of two to three small, nodding, pale lemon-yellow flowers per stem with petals swept back in the elegant reflexed form typical of the Triandrus group. It is a graceful, refined cultivar that reads better in loose drifts or rock gardens than in bold mass plantings, and it was named for its resemblance to a cluster of small hanging bells. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over time.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Elka is a compact, early-blooming Cyclamineus daffodil with reflexed white petals and a slim trumpet that opens pale lemon and fades to ivory.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Elka is a Cyclamineus-type (Division 6) miniature daffodil with narrow, sharply reflexed white petals swept back from a slender trumpet that opens soft lemon-yellow and quickly fades to near-white as the flower ages. It is one of the earliest daffodils to bloom each spring, flowering on short, sturdy stems that hold up well to wind and rain, and its small scale suits rock gardens, containers, and the front of borders. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Jenny is a Cyclamineus daffodil whose swept-back white petals and slender trumpet open pale lemon-yellow before maturing to pure white.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Jenny is a Cyclamineus-type (Division 6) daffodil with narrow, sharply reflexed white perianth segments swept back from a long, slender trumpet that opens pale lemon-yellow and gradually turns pure white as the bloom matures, giving each flower a striking two-tone effect over its life. It flowers early in the season on wiry, weather-resistant stems and naturalizes readily in light shade beneath deciduous trees and shrubs. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply.

common_name: Sun Disc Daffodil (Miniature Flat-Cupped Jonquilla Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Sun Disc is an Alec Gray-bred miniature Jonquilla daffodil with a flat, disc-like yellow cup and light fragrance.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun in fall. Sun Disc is a Jonquilla-type (Division 7) miniature daffodil bred by English hybridizer Alec Gray, bearing one or two small, rounded, uniformly yellow flowers per stem whose flat, wide-open cup gives it its name. It carries a light, sweet jonquil fragrance and its diminutive scale, rarely reaching more than a few inches tall, makes it especially well suited to rock gardens, troughs, and the front of raised beds. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply slowly over time.

common_name: Bell Song Daffodil (White Jonquilla Daffodil with Pink Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Bell Song is a fragrant, late-blooming Jonquilla daffodil with a white perianth and a small pink cup.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Bell Song is a Jonquilla-type (Division 7) daffodil bearing one to three fragrant flowers per stem, with a clean white perianth surrounding a small, rounded cup that opens pale apricot and deepens to a soft rose-pink. It blooms later than most jonquils, extending the daffodil season, and its rush-like foliage and light fragrance make it a favorite for mixed borders and cutting. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply.

common_name: Ziva Daffodil (Fragrant White Paperwhite Tazetta for Forcing)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, or force indoors in water and gravel; Ziva is the most widely grown paperwhite tazetta cultivar, prized for its heavy clusters of fragrant pure white flowers.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall in mild-winter regions, or set bulbs shallowly in bowls of gravel and water indoors any time from fall through winter for forcing. Ziva is a tazetta (Division 8) paperwhite selection bearing dense clusters of eight or more small, intensely fragrant, pure white flowers per stem on tall stalks, and it is by far the most common paperwhite sold for indoor forcing in North America because of its speed, reliability, and strong scent. It needs no chilling period and will bloom within four to six weeks of being started in water and gravel, though outdoors it is hardy only in mild-winter climates. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom before removing it, and let outdoor clumps naturalize undisturbed where winters stay frost-free.

common_name: Broadway Star Daffodil (White Split-Corona Daffodil with Yellow-Orange Collar)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Broadway Star is a modern split-corona (collar) daffodil whose flat corona opens yellow at the base and shades to soft orange at the frilled edge.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Broadway Star belongs to the split-corona group (Division 11a, "collar" daffodils), in which the corona is divided into segments that open flat against the perianth rather than standing up as a cup. Its broad white petals surround a ruffled, star-shaped corona that opens soft yellow near the throat and deepens to a warm orange at the frilled outer edge, giving the flower an almost orchid-like, papillon appearance on sturdy mid-season stems. It is a vigorous, floriferous modern cultivar valued for cutting as well as border and container display. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply.

common_name: Old Pheasant's Eye Daffodil (Fragrant Late Poet's Narcissus)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Old Pheasant's Eye is a centuries-old naturalizing form of the Poet's Narcissus with reflexed white petals and a tiny red-rimmed yellow eye, blooming latest of all daffodils.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Old Pheasant's Eye is a long-cultivated variety of the Poeticus (Division 9) group, bearing pure white, sharply reflexed perianth segments around a tiny, flat, greenish-yellow eye rimmed in bright red, carried on tall, wiry stems with an intense, sweet fragrance. It is the latest daffodil to bloom each spring, often flowering after all other divisions have finished, and it has naturalized in old farmsteads, cemeteries, and meadows across Europe and North America for centuries, thriving on neglect. Allow the foliage to die back completely after bloom before removing it, and leave established colonies undisturbed to spread by seed and offset over the years.

common_name: Van Sion Daffodil (Historic Double Yellow Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Van Sion, also known as Telamonius Plenus, is one of the oldest daffodils still in cultivation, a shaggy double sport of the wild trumpet daffodil first recorded in the early 1600s.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Van Sion, historically also sold as Telamonius Plenus, is one of the oldest named daffodils still in commerce, a fully double sport of the wild trumpet daffodil first documented in the early seventeenth century, with an irregular, shaggy mass of golden-yellow segments replacing the usual trumpet and perianth. Its untidy, informal double form and heirloom pedigree have kept it popular in old farmhouse gardens and historic plantings, where it has naturalized and persisted for generations, including in many long-abandoned homesites across the American South. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply.
